statement: For which values of the constant $c$ does the equation $x^2 + 6x + c = 2x - 3$ have two distinct real solutions?

choices.misconception: I found the discriminant correctly and reached $-4c > -4$, but I divided by $-4$ without reversing the inequality sign.
I moved $2x - 3$ to the left side but wrote the constant as $c - 3$ instead of $c + 3$, so I solved $16 - 4(c - 3) > 0$.
I used the discriminant of $x^2 + 6x + c$ and ignored the $2x - 3$ on the right side, so I solved $36 - 4c > 0$.

hints: Move everything to one side so the equation equals zero.
Rewrite it as $x^2 + 4x + (c + 3) = 0$. Two distinct real solutions means the discriminant is positive.

solutions.reliable: Subtract $2x - 3$ from both sides: $x^2 + 4x + (c + 3) = 0$. The discriminant is $4^2 - 4(1)(c + 3) = 16 - 4c - 12 = 4 - 4c$. Two distinct real solutions require $4 - 4c > 0$, so $c < 1$.
solutions.elegant: Complete the square: $x^2 + 4x + c + 3 = 0$ becomes $(x + 2)^2 = 1 - c$. There are two distinct real solutions exactly when the right side is positive, so $c < 1$.
